This birth weight is considerably smaller than the ultimate wet weight of 2457 grams [Wwi = 2457 grams] recorded for fully grown adults, indicating a substantial postnatal growth phase. During this interval, the suckling juvenile relies entirely on maternal milk before gradually incorporating solid vegetation into its diet, a shift that aligns with the seasonal availability of browse and foliage in the rocky outcrops the species inhabits.

Litter size is small, with parturition yielding one to two pups per litter [N_R_i = one to two pups per litter]. Furthermore, the relatively slow pace of sexual maturation, spanning over 16 months, reflects the energetic demands of attaining the adult body mass of 2457 grams [Wwi = 2457 grams], a threshold that must be crossed before reproductive effort can be sustained. By contrast, maximum lifespan in the wild is considerably longer, with the oldest documented individual of the closely related Procavia capensis reaching 12 years [am = 12 years] at a temperature of 36.7 °C [T = 36.7 °C]. Basal metabolic rate, measured via respirometry during the inactive phase of the daily activity cycle at a core temperature of 36.7 °C [T = 36.7 °C], averages 720 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 720 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. The measurement was obtained from post-absorptive, resting adults during the thermoneutral zone.

With a single annual litter and a litter size of one or two pups, the annual reproductive output of Heterohyrax brucei is constrained to a small number of offspring. This modest reproductive allocation is invested in precocial young that benefit from an extended gestation and a relatively short weaning period, optimizing survival in the species' stable but resource-limited kopje habitats. The synchronized timing of parturition with peak forage availability further supports neonatal survival, while the social dynamics of the colony influence which individuals successfully breed each year.
